profile.name: Adnan Bashir
profile.description: Adnan Bashir — AI and time-series researcher, cybersecurity educator, and PhD candidate. Teaching and research at the intersection of intelligence, security, and visual exploration.

hero.intro: I’m Adnan Bashir. I study how machines learn from changing data, teach cybersecurity, and build tools that make complex ideas visible.

about.heading:
Between intelligence,
security, and curiosity.
about.lead: My work connects machine learning, time-series analysis, and cybersecurity education.
about.secondary: I’m interested in the moments when data changes—and how we can help people understand what that change means.
about.note: I bring research into the classroom through numerical examples and small, inspectable experiments. My work moves between statistical methods, software tools, and the visual language we use to explain them.

items.title: SegStream
items.subtitle: Time-series segmentation & state discovery
items.description: Investigating how to divide a multivariate time series into meaningful segments and identify the states within it. The work brings boundary detection and state discovery into a shared experimental workflow.

notes.heading: The question
notes.text: Where does one behavior end, and another begin?

notes.heading: The approach
notes.text: Inspect neighboring windows, score potential boundaries, and explore how segments relate to recurring states.

items.title: DRUM-Ext
items.subtitle: Window comparisons & boundary scoring
items.description: Exploring how comparisons between neighboring windows reveal changes in a signal. Experiments examine window size, feature behavior, and boundary scores across different datasets.

notes.heading: What I examine
notes.text: The influence of window length, feature changes, and the tolerance used to match detected boundaries.

notes.heading: Why it matters
notes.text: A boundary should reflect a change in the underlying behavior, with evidence that can be inspected.

items.title: Statistical change detection
items.subtitle: From test statistics to interpretable experiments
items.description: Studying nearest-neighbor two-sample tests and ISSD-related methods to understand the evidence behind a detected change. Numerical walkthroughs and visual experiments make assumptions and test behavior easier to inspect.

notes.heading: The question
notes.text: Do two windows contain evidence of the same distribution?

notes.heading: The explanation
notes.text: Work through the statistic, its null behavior, and what changes under an alternative hypothesis.

mathematics.heading:
A few equations.
Many connections.
mathematics.intro: From detecting change in a stream to learning from a network. One equation from my published research, alongside five foundations that help connect these ideas.

items.title: Recognizing a changing stream
items.label: From my research · DRUM
items.description: DRUM combines changes in a stream’s mean, variability, and crossings of its running mean to support unsupervised detection of regime shifts.
items.notation: i indexes the n variables; j and k are the starting positions of two windows of length d + 1. The deltas are absolute differences in window means, standard deviations, and running-mean crossing counts. The weights α, β, γ lie in [0, 1]; the paper does not require them to sum to one.

items.title: The capacity of a connection
items.label: Foundation · Information theory
items.description: Bandwidth and noise set the limits of communication. Those limits shape how sensing, learning, and inference move across a network.
items.notation: C is capacity in bits per second; B is bandwidth in hertz; S/N is the signal-to-noise power ratio in linear units. This form applies to a band-limited additive white Gaussian noise channel with an average signal-power constraint.
items.sourceLabel: Shannon · A Mathematical Theory of Communication, 1948

items.title: The mathematics of waiting
items.label: Foundation · Computer networks
items.description: Every packet and inference request spends time inside a system. Little’s law connects that time to throughput and the amount of work in flight.
items.notation: L is the mean number of items in the system; λ is the effective arrival rate; W is the mean time spent there. Use consistent system boundaries and a stable regime with finite long-run averages.
items.sourceLabel: Little · A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW, 1961

items.title: Evidence becomes belief
items.label: Foundation · Probabilistic inference
items.description: An unusual observation is evidence, not a verdict. Bayesian reasoning combines observations with prior knowledge to update a hypothesis about the system.
items.notation: A is a hypothesis, such as an anomalous state; E is observed evidence. P(A) is the prior and P(A | E) is the posterior. This event-based form requires P(E) > 0.

items.title: Learning from prediction
items.label: Foundation · Machine learning
items.description: A model learns by assigning probability to observed outcomes. Cross-entropy turns that mismatch into a training objective for tasks such as traffic classification.
items.notation: For one example, y_c is the target probability for class c, p̂_c is the predicted probability, and K is the number of classes. Both probability vectors sum to one. Predictions must be positive wherever targets are positive. Natural logarithms give loss in nats.

items.title: Measuring uncertainty
items.label: Foundation · Information & learning
items.description: Entropy describes uncertainty in a distribution. It provides a shared mathematical language for communication patterns and probabilistic predictions.
items.notation: X is a discrete random variable with probability mass function p(x). Base-two logarithms give bits, and 0 log 0 is defined as 0. Entropy alone does not establish that traffic is anomalous or that a model is calibrated.
items.sourceLabel: Shannon · A Mathematical Theory of Communication, 1948
